The complete workflow

From broad field to defensible chapter

  1. Frame
    Turn the thesis problem into searchable concepts.

    Define population or unit, phenomenon, mechanisms, outcomes, place, period, and study designs.

  2. Find
    Search widely enough to avoid a convenience sample.

    Combine databases, Google Scholar, review articles, backward/forward citation chaining, key journals, working papers, and Malaysian repositories.

  3. Filter
    Apply pre-declared inclusion criteria.

    Record the database, exact query, date, results, screening reason, and version of every retained work.

  4. Map
    Extract comparable evidence.

    Code theory, mechanism, context, data, identification strategy, variables, findings, limitations, and relevance.

  5. Synthesise
    Organise by debate, mechanism, method, or finding.

    Use chronology only when intellectual change over time is itself part of the argument.

  6. Position
    Make the gap and framework earn their place.

    Show what remains unresolved and how the thesis design resolves or narrows it.

Professor's source notes

The inherited teaching spine

  • Ask “What has been done?” before claiming novelty.
  • Do not reinvent the wheel; identify variables, methods, strengths, and weaknesses.
  • Use thematic and funnelled writing.
  • Distinguish references (cited) from bibliography (read).
  • Snowball from recent reviews and seminal papers.
  • Keep searching; use alerts and key-journal monitoring.

Adapted from the three lecture-note files supplied with this project.

Recommended next: clarify what a literature review must accomplish.

Module 01

What a literature review is—and is not

The chapter is a reasoned synthesis of an evidence field. Its unit of organisation is the problem or debate, not the paper.

A literature review searches, selects, appraises, compares, and synthesises prior knowledge to establish the thesis's conceptual position, empirical warrant, and research design.

It isIt is not
A map of explanations, evidence, and unresolved tensions.A paragraph-by-paragraph list of who said what.
A transparent account of how the evidence base was found and bounded.Whatever papers happened to appear first in Scholar.
A critical appraisal of claims relative to designs and contexts.A ritual complaint that every study has “small sample size.”
A bridge from theory and evidence to research questions and methods.A detached history chapter that never reaches the thesis.

Why a PhD needs it

Orient
Define the vocabulary, constructs, boundaries, and schools of thought.
Accumulate
Show which findings are robust, conditional, disputed, or missing.
Interrogate
Separate evidence from assertion and design limits from substantive disagreement.
Position
Demonstrate the thesis's incremental, theoretical, empirical, contextual, or methodological contribution.
Design
Justify variables, mechanisms, identification, data, cases, and measures.

Choose the review mode

Narrative critical review

Best for a thesis chapter that must reconstruct debates, theories, and evidence across heterogeneous designs. Still document the search and selection process.

Systematic review

Use when the question, eligibility rules, searches, screening, and synthesis can be made reproducible. Use PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S as reporting guides; do not claim “systematic” merely because many papers were read.

Scoping review

Use to map concepts, evidence types, and research activity when the field is broad or emerging. It is not a shortcut for weak critical appraisal.

Meta-analysis

Use when comparable effect estimates can be statistically combined and heterogeneity can be modelled. It is a synthesis method, not a synonym for literature review.

Five-minute diagnostic

Defend the review design

Write one sentence naming your review mode and one sentence explaining why it matches your question and evidence.

Module 02

Search like an economist, document like an auditor

Discovery can be exploratory. The final search must be reproducible enough that a reader can see what was in scope and what could have been missed.

The six-pass search

  1. Scope. Translate the research problem into 3–5 concept blocks: phenomenon, outcome, mechanism, population/unit, geography.
  2. Seed. Locate recent review articles, handbook chapters, seminal papers, and key Malaysian studies.
  3. Search. Run adapted strings in EconLit, Scopus/Web of Science, disciplinary databases, repositories, and Scholar.
  4. Chain. Search backward through references and forward through “Cited by”; use “Related articles” to find semantic neighbours.
  5. Screen. Apply inclusion/exclusion criteria first to title/abstract, then full text. Record one defensible reason per exclusion.
  6. Refresh. Re-run the search near submission; set alerts for core queries, authors, and journals.

Search record minimum

  • Database and platform
  • Exact query as run
  • Date searched
  • Fields and filters
  • Results exported
  • Duplicates removed
  • Eligibility rule
  • Screening decision

PRISMA-S provides 16 reporting items for literature searches. Use it as a transparency checklist even when the thesis review is not a full systematic review.

Google Scholar query builder

Build a concept-block query

Interactive

In Scholar, spaces imply AND; capitalised OR (or |) broadens; quotes preserve a phrase; a minus sign excludes a term. Long nested database strings may behave unpredictably, so test each block and inspect whether known “sentinel” papers appear.

Google Scholar Boolean field manual

  1. Start short. Use 2–4 core ideas, not the full research question.
  2. Phrase. Put stable multiword terms in quotation marks.
  3. Synonyms. Join variants with capitalised OR.
  4. Exclude sparingly. Use -term; each exclusion risks removing relevant papers.
  5. Target. Try author:"name", an exact title in quotes, or Advanced Search for author, title, publication, and year fields.
  6. Retrieve. Check [PDF]/[HTML], library links, “All versions,” institutional repositories, and lawful author copies.
  7. Chain. Use “Cited by,” “Related articles,” and reference lists.
  8. Monitor. Create an email alert and rerun the dated search before submission.

Guide: Google Scholar Search Help

Worked search: B40 food expenditure

Question. How do food-price changes affect food expenditure and diet adjustment among B40 households in Malaysia?

Blocks. price/inflation · expenditure/consumption/diet · B40/low-income/household · Malaysia.

("food price" OR "food inflation") (expenditure OR consumption OR diet) (B40 OR "low income" OR household) Malaysia

Iteration. If B40 is too restrictive, remove it, screen on Malaysian household samples, then search author: for recurring DOSM/HES researchers.

Sentinel check. The query should retrieve at least one known Malaysian household-expenditure study and one paper using Household Expenditure Survey data.

Module 03

Use AI to widen and interrogate—not to invent—the evidence base

AI is useful for query expansion, screening support, extraction, comparison, and challenge. Bibliographic facts and substantive claims still require source-level verification.

AI may proposesynonyms, JEL terms, screening labels, comparison axes, counterarguments
The researcher must verifyexistence, DOI, authorship, year, sample, method, estimate, quotation, and interpretation

A source-grounded AI workflow

  1. Plan without citations. Ask AI to decompose the question into concepts, synonyms, mechanisms, JEL codes, and candidate inclusion rules.
  2. Search outside the chatbot. Use the terms in scholarly databases and export real records.
  3. Ground. Upload lawfully obtained papers or abstracts to a source-grounded tool; constrain answers to selected sources.
  4. Extract with evidence. Require page/section pointers and “not reported” instead of guesses.
  5. Adversarial check. Ask what evidence contradicts the emerging story, which contexts differ, and what design limitations change inference.
  6. Audit. Randomly verify cells, quotations, and classifications; keep a correction log.

Tool roles, not tool worship

Discovery

Scholar, EconLit, Scopus/Web of Science, Semantic Scholar feeds, citation networks.

Management

Zotero or another reference manager: deduplicate, tag, attach files, cite, and preserve metadata.

Grounded analysis

Gemini Notebook: compare the sources you selected, generate tables and mind maps, then verify each output against citations.

Writing support

Outline, test structure, identify unsupported transitions, or revise clarity after the researcher's claims are fixed.

Prompt studio

Compose a high-control LR prompt


        


        
Complete prompt: source-grounded chapter synthesis
ROLE: Act as a critical economics literature-review assistant. Do not write as an authority beyond the supplied evidence.

OBJECTIVE: Help me construct a synthesis for [SUBSECTION] on [TOPIC] that leads to [RESEARCH QUESTION].

EVIDENCE BOUNDARY: Use only the sources I provide. Do not invent or complete missing citations. If a fact is absent, write “not reported”. Attach a source name and page/section pointer to every substantive claim.

ANALYTICAL TASKS:
1. Group studies by mechanism, theoretical prediction, identification strategy, context, and direction of finding—not by author.
2. Separate descriptive association, causal evidence, model-based simulation, and theoretical proposition.
3. Identify genuine convergence, conditional agreement, contradiction, and incomparable evidence.
4. Explain whether disagreement is plausibly due to data period, sample, measurement, institutional context, functional form, or identification.
5. Identify what the evidence cannot establish.
6. Draft a synthesis outline using claim → comparative evidence → interpretation → implication → bridge.

OUTPUT:
A. Evidence map table.
B. Three candidate synthesis claims, each with support and counter-evidence.
C. A 250-word draft labelled “provisional” with citations in [APA 7].
D. Verification checklist listing every claim I must inspect in the original source.

QUALITY RULES: Preserve uncertainty and effect direction. Do not call a correlation causal. Do not use fabricated quotations, DOI, page numbers, sample sizes, or coefficients. Avoid stock phrases such as “it is important to note,” “delve,” and “this underscores”.


        
Rule of custody: Never upload confidential manuscripts, restricted microdata, identifiable respondent material, or copyrighted files when licence or institutional policy does not permit it. Record the tool, date, purpose, prompt, sources, and verification performed.

      


      

        

          
Module 04

          
A Chapter 2 architecture that moves from field to thesis

          
A strong sequence is not universal, but every section should answer a different question and narrow toward the study's design.

        


        

          
2.1
Introduction and scope
State the chapter's purpose, boundaries, review approach, and organising logic. Preview the debates—not the conclusion in full.
Model opening: “This chapter reviews theoretical and empirical explanations for household adjustment to food-price shocks, with particular attention to distributional heterogeneity and Malaysia's B40 classification.”

          
2.2
Concepts and topical context
Define contested constructs, units, and institutional features. Avoid turning this into a dictionary: compare definitions and justify the one used.

          
2.3
Theoretical literature
Present the mechanisms that generate predictions. Compare assumptions, scope conditions, and competing propositions; derive observable implications.

          
2.4
International empirical evidence
Synthesise by mechanism, design, outcome, or debate. Explain why estimates differ and which evidence is most informative for the thesis.

          
2.5
Malaysian and institutional evidence
Move from transferable international mechanisms to Malaysia's institutions, data, policy, and population. Do not isolate local work as a ceremonial list.

          
2.6
Method and measurement literature
Locate here when methodological choices shape the substantive debate; otherwise justify them in Chapter 3 and cross-reference.

          
2.7
Synthesis and literature gap
State what is known, where inference stops, why the unresolved issue matters, and exactly how the thesis addresses it.

          
2.8
Framework and propositions
Integrate theory, concepts, variables, context, and expected relationships. Ensure every arrow has a written mechanism and later measurement plan.

          
2.9
Chapter summary
Summarise the argument—not each section—and hand the reader to the research design.

        


        

          
Alternative inherited from the lecture notes: a theory-led brain-drain chapter can move from human capital and random utility theory → early and continuing debates → brain-gain hypothesis → datasets → theoretical models of nonreturn → empirical determinants → variable selection. The organising principle is intellectual dependency, not a compulsory template.

        

      


      

        

          
Module 05

          
Write across studies, not down a bibliography

          
The paragraph's first sentence should usually make a literature-level claim. Citations then support, qualify, or challenge it.

        


        

          
Weak: catalogue
Author A (2019) studied minimum wages and employment. Author B (2020) studied minimum wages and employment. Author C (2022) examined Malaysia and found a significant result. Author D (2023) also studied youth.
  • No organising claim
  • No comparison of designs or contexts
  • “Significant” without magnitude or direction
  • Thesis relevance is invisible

          
Stronger: synthesis
Estimates of youth employment responses to minimum-wage increases depend heavily on how studies address policy endogeneity and labour-market adjustment. Designs exploiting subnational timing tend to identify short-run employment effects, whereas firm- or worker-level panels reveal adjustment through hours, turnover, and formality. Malaysian evidence is especially difficult to compare because national wage floors changed alongside sectoral and regional conditions; the relevant gap is therefore not another average association, but credible identification of heterogeneous adjustment among low-wage youth.
  • Claim leads
  • Methods explain disagreement
  • Context narrows the inference
  • Gap follows from the synthesis

        


        

          

            
The CECIB paragraph

            

              
C
Claim: a literature-level proposition.

              
E
Evidence: multiple relevant studies, weighted by design.

              
C
Comparison: agreement, contrast, condition, or evolution.

              
I
Interpretation: why evidence differs and what it can establish.

              
B
Bridge: implication for the next debate or the thesis.

            

          

          

            
Funnel at three scales

            
    
              
  1. Chapter: broad problem → theories → international evidence → Malaysian context → gap → framework.
    2. 
              
  2. Section: dominant explanation → alternatives → boundary conditions → unresolved issue.
    3. 
              
  3. Paragraph: synthesis claim → evidence → comparison → interpretation → bridge.
    4. 
            

            
Do not confuse criticism with negativity. A critical review judges what a claim is warranted to mean, given the data, design, measurement, and context.

          

        


        

          
Rewrite clinic
Turn four authors into one argument
Draft a CECIB paragraph. Use at least one contrast connector and one design-based explanation.

          
        

      


      

        

          
Module 06

          
Write Malaysian literature as an analytical context, not a geographic appendix

          
The local review should show which mechanisms travel, which are institution-specific, what Malaysian data can identify, and why the thesis's context changes the inference.

        


        

          
1International regularity
What mechanism or empirical pattern appears across settings?

          
2Institutional translation
How do Malaysian policy, labour-market, demographic, spatial, and data institutions alter it?

          
3Local evidence
What have Malaysian studies measured, with which designs and populations?

          
4Comparative limit
Where do scope, measurement, period, or identification prevent a firm conclusion?

          
5Thesis warrant
What exact uncertainty remains, and how will this study reduce it?

        


        

          

            
Worked paragraph anatomy

            
Only a small Malaysian literature examines household responses to severe flood risk. Existing studies converge on the importance of preparedness and information, but examine different actors: victims, emergency agencies, and community-warning systems. Because most evidence concerns floods of typical magnitude and relies on reported experience, it does not establish whether behaviour transfers to rarer compound disasters. International evacuation studies offer testable mechanisms—risk perception, notice, shelter access, and household constraints—but their institutional settings cannot be imported unchanged.

            
Adapted and paraphrased from the Malaysian flood-literature example in the supplied lecture notes.

          

          

            
Malaysia-specific search layer

            
    
              
  • Search Malaysia, Malaysian, state names, and institutional terms separately.
    • 
              
  • Check DOSM, Bank Negara Malaysia, ministries, parliamentary and policy reports, and university repositories.
    • 
              
  • Use MySitasi/MyCite lineage to inspect Malaysian scholarly journals, but still appraise journal practices and article quality.
    • 
              
  • Search authors and research groups when local terminology differs from international keywords.
    • 
              
  • Record whether local evidence is peer-reviewed, working paper, thesis, report, or administrative documentation.
    •

Module 07

          
A gap is a warranted unresolved problem—not “few studies exist”

          
The review must establish the gap, its consequence for knowledge or policy, and why the proposed study can address it.

        


        

          
Evidence
Missing or thin evidence
A relevant population, period, outcome, or institution has not been credibly studied.
Test: would one more descriptive paper fill it?

          
Contradiction
Unresolved disagreement
Findings point in different directions and the source of heterogeneity is not understood.
Test: are studies actually comparable?

          
Method
Identification or measurement
Prior designs cannot distinguish competing explanations, or key constructs are measured poorly.
Test: does your design materially improve inference?

          
Theory
Mechanism or boundary
A theory does not specify the context in which its prediction holds, or rival theories imply similar observed patterns.
Test: what observable implication separates them?

          
Context
Institutional transferability
Evidence comes from settings whose institutions differ in ways that matter to the mechanism.
Test: explain why place changes theory—not merely that it is new.

          
Integration
Disconnected literatures
Two bodies of work study connected mechanisms but do not speak to each other.
Test: does integration produce a new prediction?

          
Temporal
Structural change
Technology, policy, shocks, or institutions make older relationships uncertain.
Test: specify what changed and when.

          
Implementation
Knowledge–action gap
Effects are known, but adoption, scale, incidence, or political-economy constraints remain unclear.
Test: is the question researchable rather than advisory?

        


        
Gap claim =established pattern+bounded limitation or tension+consequence+researchable response


        

          
Weak gap
There are few studies on food prices and B40 households in Malaysia. Therefore, this study fills the gap.

          
Defensible gap
Malaysian expenditure studies document food-budget pressure, but aggregate Engel-curve estimates do not identify whether households adjust quantities, quality, or category composition when prices change. This limits distributional policy design because equal expenditure changes can conceal unequal nutritional responses. The thesis addresses this measurement and mechanism gap by linking item-level prices to household expenditure shares across income groups.

        


        

          
Gap stress test
Can the proposed gap survive five objections?
0/5

          
          
          
          
          
        

      


      

        

          
Module 08

          
Choose the framework for the job

          
Framework labels are used inconsistently across disciplines. Define what the figure does, then ensure its nodes and arrows correspond to written mechanisms, measures, and methods.

        


        

          
FrameworkPrimary questionContainsUse when

          
TheoreticalWhich formal or established explanation generates the prediction?Theory, assumptions, mechanisms, propositionsThe study tests, extends, contrasts, or operationalises theory.

          
ConceptualHow are the study's constructs expected to relate?Constructs, pathways, moderators, contextSeveral theories or empirical insights must be integrated.

          
AnalyticalHow will evidence be interpreted or decomposed?Categories, dimensions, mechanisms, decision rulesThe study needs a lens for qualitative, policy, institutional, or mixed evidence.

          
ResearchHow do problem, questions, data, methods, outputs, and contribution align?RQ/RO, data, method, analysis, output, outcomeA proposal or thesis needs an end-to-end roadmap.

        


        

          
Decision aid
If you may show only one framework
Recommendation

          

            
            
          

          

        


        

          

            
Default rule when only one is permitted

            
Use an integrated conceptual framework grounded explicitly in theory. It is usually the most informative single figure because it can show constructs, expected relationships, mechanisms, moderators, and context while citing the theories that justify them.

            
Exception: if the thesis contribution is a direct formal test or extension of one theory, use the theoretical framework. If the institution requires a “research framework,” retain that label but build a theory-grounded conceptual core and explain the terminology.

          

          

            
Arrow audit

            
    
              
  • Every arrow has a mechanism stated in prose.
    • 
              
  • Every construct has an operational definition later.
    • 
              
  • Direction and feedback are intentional.
    • 
              
  • Mediators, moderators, controls, and outcomes are not conflated.
    • 
              
  • No decorative variable appears only because a past study used it.
    • 
              
  • The empirical design can evaluate the relationships shown.
    • 
            

          

        


        

          
Worked example from the supplied notes

          
Wage determination: theory → concept → variable

          

            
Theory or model
Human capital / Mincer earnings
Hedonic wage theory
On-the-job training
Labour-market discrimination
Monopoly union model

            
Concept
Human-capital investment
Working conditions
Training accumulation
Minority-group penalty
Union bargaining

            
Candidate operationalisation
Years/level of education
Occupation risk or job attributes
Training duration
Gender, ethnicity, citizenship
Union membership

          

          
Variables do not “come from the literature” in the abstract; they operationalise theoretically meaningful concepts within a specified empirical design.

        

      


      

        

          
Module 09

          
The evidence matrix is a thinking instrument

          
A useful matrix makes studies comparable and exposes patterns. A giant table of copied abstracts merely relocates the reading problem.

        


        

          
BibliographicAuthor, year, title, outlet, DOI/URL

          
SubstantiveQuestion, theory, mechanism, context

          
DesignData, sample, period, identification, variables

          
InferenceFinding, magnitude, uncertainty, limitation

          
SynthesisTheme, contradiction, relevance, quote/page

        


        

        

          

            
StudyQuestion / theoryContext & dataDesignFindingLimitation / use

            
              
Illustrative A
Household price response		Consumer demand; substitution and income effectsMalaysia HES; B40 householdsDemand system; repeated cross-sectionsFood shares rise as budgets tighten; category responses differAssociation/structure depends on price measurement; motivates item-level linkage

              
Illustrative B
Food-price shock		Vulnerability and consumption smoothingRegional household panelPanel fixed effects / shock exposureAdjustment occurs through quantity and quality marginsInstitutional transfer to Malaysia uncertain; supplies mechanism and outcomes

            
          

        

        
Illustrative rows demonstrate the schema; they are not bibliographic records and must not be cited as studies.


        

          
Matrix rules
  • One row per study or analytically distinct result.
  • Use standardised labels; preserve effect direction and unit.
  • Write “not reported,” never infer missing sample or method details.
  • Keep a locator for every quotation or numerical claim.
  • Code relevance to a planned synthesis claim.
  • Audit a random sample after any AI-assisted extraction.

          
From matrix to prose
  1. Filter one theme or mechanism.
  2. Sort by design strength or context—not alphabetically.
  3. Mark convergence, contradiction, and incomparable evidence.
  4. Write a claim that survives the counter-evidence.
  5. Cite representative and decisive studies, not every row mechanically.

Gemini Notebook: build matrices and mind maps from controlled sources

          
Google renamed NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook in July 2026. The workflow remains source-grounded: you select the corpus, generate an artefact, then verify every important claim.

        


        

          

            
Tutorial A

            
Create an LR summary table

            
    
              
  1. Create one notebook for one review question or coherent subtopic.
    2. 
              
  2. Upload the final screened PDFs/records; use clear filenames such as Author_Year_ShortTitle.pdf.
    3.

    4.

    5.

    6.

    7. 
              
  7. Use the three-dot menu → Export to Sheets. Content goes to one tab and citations to another.

    9. 
            

          

          

            
Tutorial B

            
Create an LR mind map

            
    
              
  1. Select a coherent source set; mixed topics create shallow branches.
    2. 
              
  2. In Chat, select the Mind Map chip.
    3. 
              
  3. Open the generated map in Studio; expand/collapse branches and select nodes to ask source-grounded questions.
    4.

    7. 
            

            
Official Mind Maps guide

          

        


        
Gemini Notebook prompt: thesis literature matrix
Create a data table with one row per included study and these columns:
1. Full citation exactly as shown in the source
2. Research question
3. Theory or conceptual mechanism
4. Country/institutional context
5. Data source, period, unit of analysis, and sample size
6. Outcome and key explanatory variables
7. Empirical or analytical method
8. Identification assumptions
9. Main finding with direction, magnitude, and uncertainty where reported
10. Authors' stated limitation
11. My synthesis code: convergence / contradiction / boundary / method issue / contextual relevance
12. Exact page or section supporting each extracted claim

Use only the selected sources. If an item is absent, write “not reported”; do not infer it. Keep descriptive association separate from causal evidence. Flag any cell whose interpretation is uncertain.


        
Gemini Notebook prompt: argument-centred mind map
Using only the selected sources, construct a mind-map plan for the literature review on [TOPIC]. Place the research problem at the centre. Use first-level branches for: theories, mechanisms, empirical findings, methods/identification, institutional contexts, contradictions, and unresolved questions. Under each branch, name the supporting sources and distinguish established evidence from author interpretation. Add a “missing or weakly connected evidence” branch. Do not treat citation frequency as evidence strength.


        
Verification rule: Gemini Notebook can be inaccurate, and source import can omit features such as Google-file footnotes or comments. Use the generated table/map as a draft analytical artefact, not as a citable authority.

        
Current product guidance: Create a notebook and Data Tables · Sources and limitations · NotebookLM rename

      


      

        

          
Module 11

          
Appraise the article and the outlet—never outsource judgement to one metric

          
Indexing is useful evidence of editorial screening, not a guarantee that every article is strong. New, regional, or specialised journals can be credible without elite metrics.

        


        

          
1Identity
Verify title, ISSN, publisher, domain, archive, and contact information. Watch for cloned or confusingly similar titles.

          
2Process
Look for specific peer review, ethics, corrections/retractions, authorship, data, conflicts, and fee policies.

          
3People
Check whether editors are identifiable, qualified, and plausibly involved; sample their institutional pages.

          
4Trace
Verify claims directly in EconLit, DOAJ, Scopus Sources, Web of Science Master Journal List, and relevant Malaysian systems.

          
5Article
Judge question, theory, data, design, transparency, inference, robustness, and reporting—regardless of logo.

        


        

          

            
Credibility signals

            
  • Scope and ownership are clear.
  • ISSN and journal identity match independent records.
  • Peer-review model and editorial policies are specific.
  • Fees are disclosed before submission.
  • Editorial board members are verifiable.
  • Corrections, retractions, and archives are maintained.
  • Indexing claims can be confirmed at the indexer's site.
  • Published articles show plausible timelines and competent methods.

          

          

            
Red flags requiring investigation

            
  • Spam invitation unrelated to your field.
  • Guaranteed acceptance or implausibly rapid review.
  • Hidden fees or payment demanded after acceptance.
  • Fake metrics, invented indexing, or hijacked journal identity.
  • Very broad scope with weak editorial expertise.
  • Copied website text, broken archives, or unverifiable address.
  • Board members who deny involvement or cannot be identified.
  • Systematic mismatch between claims, methods, and editorial quality.

          

        


        

          
Journal triage
Evidence-based credibility check
Not assessed

Module 12

          
Spot AI-shaped prose by its evidential behaviour, not a magic word list

          
Style clues can trigger questions, but they do not prove authorship. The strongest audit tests citation custody, source fidelity, conceptual precision, and the writer's ability to explain decisions.

        


        

          
Language
Lexical clichés
“Delve,” “tapestry,” “landscape,” “realm,” “multifaceted,” “pivotal,” “robust,” “nuanced,” “underscore,” “shed light,” “ever-evolving.”
A word is not evidence. Look for clustering and misfit.

          
Structure
Template cadence
Repeated triads, mirrored paragraphs, mechanical headings, “not only…but also,” forced contrasts, recap after every short section.

          
Evidence
Citation theatre
Nonexistent references; real citations attached to wrong claims; page-free quotations; vague “studies show”; precise numbers without traceable sources.

          
Reasoning
Analytical emptiness
Generic praise/criticism, no magnitude, no design distinction, causality from correlation, contradictions smoothed into “mixed findings.”

          
Voice
Unearned authority
High certainty without evidence, universal policy prescriptions, fabricated consensus, abrupt expertise beyond the writer's demonstrated command.

          
Formatting
Tool residue
Placeholder brackets, chat preambles, markdown remnants, fake links/DOIs, inconsistent citation styles, unexplained tables, or repeated concluding slogans.

        


        

          

            
The viva-style authorship check

            
  1. Ask the writer to retrieve the source behind a randomly selected claim.
  2. Ask why two studies were grouped and a third excluded.
  3. Ask what changed between matrix, outline, and draft.
  4. Ask which evidence most seriously threatens the paragraph's claim.
  5. Inspect notes, version history, prompts, and correction log where policy permits.

          

          

            
Revise AI-shaped prose

            
  • Replace generic topic sentences with falsifiable synthesis claims.
  • Attach every claim to verified evidence and locators.
  • State effect direction, magnitude, uncertainty, and design.
  • Name the mechanism linking evidence to interpretation.
  • Preserve disagreement and boundary conditions.
  • Delete transitions that do no logical work.
  • Read aloud for repetitive rhythm and inflated diction.

          

        


        
Fairness warning: AI detectors can misclassify human and AI-assisted text and should not be the sole basis for adverse action. Turnitin itself requires human judgement; published studies report reliability and fairness problems, particularly in some non-native-English settings.

Module 13

          
Instructor-ready seminars, tutorials, and assessment

          
Use the modules independently or as a four-session sequence. Student inputs are stored locally and can be exported as a Markdown learning log.

        


        

          
Seminar 1 · 120 min
Find and bound the field
Before: one-page problem statement. In class: concept blocks, Scholar query tournament, sentinel-paper test, screening criteria. Exit: search protocol and search log.

          
Seminar 2 · 120 min
From reading to synthesis
Before: six papers in a matrix. In class: catalogue diagnosis, CECIB rewrite, contradiction mapping, evidence weighting. Exit: two synthesis paragraphs and a matrix revision.

          
Seminar 3 · 120 min
Gap and framework clinic
Before: one gap claim and one diagram. In class: gap objections, theory→concept→measure chain, arrow audit, framework choice. Exit: defensible gap and integrated framework.

          
Seminar 4 · 120 min
AI, integrity, and chapter defence
Before: AI-assisted extraction plus correction log. In class: hallucinated citation hunt, source-custody viva, prose forensics, journal triage. Exit: AI disclosure and chapter quality plan.

Supervisor conference questions

            
  1. What is the chapter's one-sentence argument?
  2. Which literature is outside scope, and why?
  3. Which three studies most constrain the thesis claim?
  4. Where does evidence disagree, and what explains it?
  5. What is known internationally but uncertain in Malaysia?
  6. Which theory gives each major arrow in the framework?
  7. What finding would make the gap disappear?
  8. What changed after AI output was checked?

Working glossary

          
Bibliography
Works consulted; not necessarily cited. A reference list contains works cited in the text.
Citation chaining
Backward search through references and forward search through citing works.
Construct
An abstract concept represented through one or more measures.
Evidence gap
A consequential uncertainty demonstrated by the reviewed evidence.
Identification
The assumptions and variation that allow a parameter or causal effect to be learned from data.
Mechanism
The process through which an explanatory factor generates an outcome.
Sentinel paper
A known relevant study used to test whether a search strategy has adequate recall.
Synthesis
An integrated claim about a body of evidence, including convergence, heterogeneity, contradiction, and limits.
